text: 5-year-old boy. The patient is presented by his mother for a well-child visit. The boy was born at 39 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery, is currently up to date on all vaccines, and is meeting all developmental milestones. His mother reports that he has been generally doing well with no concerns. No family history of cardiovascular disease. The boy does not take any medications.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Coarctation of the Aorta (Incidental Finding)

Since you are a 5-year-old boy with normal blood pressure measurements and a well-child visit presentation, this hypertension evaluation was likely triggered by screening or a specific finding. Coarctation of the Aorta is the most critical secondary cause of hypertension in children, but it is often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally when blood pressure is measured in both arms and legs or via imaging. The normal initial labs and metabolic panel help rule out renal parenchymal disease. The abdominal ultrasound requested will evaluate the renal arteries, but the definitive diagnosis for aortic coarctation requires visualization of the aorta itself, which is why I have already requested the Abdominal_Aorta_Ultrasound images. Based on the clinical picture of a young child with systemic hypertension, the absence of other metabolic causes, and the high suspicion for a structural aortic anomaly, the diagnosis is Coarctation
